/-!
# Erdős Problem 3

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/3](https://www.erdosproblems.com/3)
-/

namespace Erdos3

/--
If $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ has $\sum_{n \in A}\frac 1 n = \infty$, then must $A$ contain arbitrarily
long arithmetic progressions?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_3 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ A : Set ℕ,
    (¬ Summable fun a : A ↦ 1 / (a : ℝ)) →
    ∃ᶠ (k : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ∃ S ⊆ A, S.IsAPOfLength k := by
  sorry

-- TODO(firsching): add the various known bounds as variants.

end Erdos3

reformulations.difference: Lean allows zero in A, expresses divergence as nonsummability of a real-valued subtype family, and uses frequently-atTop AP lengths instead of explicitly requiring a positive-difference progression of every prescribed length.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: All reciprocal terms are nonnegative, so nonsummability is equivalent to partial sums tending to +∞. Since 1/0 = 0 in ℝ, deleting zero preserves summability. Deleting zero also preserves arbitrarily long APs: take the last k terms of a (k+1)-term positive-difference progression. IsAPOfLength requires ENat.card S = k, which excludes zero common difference for k ≥ 2. Frequently atTop on ℕ means unbounded lengths; truncating longer progressions gives every requested length, and the converse is immediate. The full equivalence with the positive-integer, divergent-partial-sum, explicit-positive-difference formulation was proved as ReviewErdos3.full_source_equivalence in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.
